title: Searching: Core Concepts
description: Fundamentals of searching in data structures.

questions.question: What is the definition of 'searching' in data structures?
options: The process of sorting data in ascending order
The process of locating a specific record with a particular key value
The process of deleting a record from a dataset
The process of inserting new data into a structure
questions.explanation: Searching is defined as locating a specific record by its key value. If the key is found, the search succeeds and the record is retrieved.

questions.question: In the context of searching, what is a 'key'?
options: A password used to encrypt data
The first element of an array
The specific value you are looking for in a collection of data
The index of the last element
questions.explanation: A key is the specific value used to identify the item being searched for. The search aims to find this key within the dataset.

questions.question: Real life example: You look for the name 'Maria' by scanning each contact in your phone in order. What type of search is this?
questions.explanation: Scanning each item in order until you find the target is Linear Search — it checks elements one by one without assuming any order.

questions.question: If a key appears multiple times in the data, what does a basic search usually return?
options: It fails because duplicates are not allowed
It usually returns one occurrence, often the first found
It resorts the data and searches again
questions.explanation: Basic search algorithms typically return a single match. Finding all duplicates requires a different approach or repeated searches.

questions.question: Why is efficient searching especially important for large databases?
options: It makes queries fast even when millions of records exist
questions.explanation: Efficient searching keeps large systems usable by enabling fast lookups. Slow search performance can make large databases impractical for real-time use.

title: Linear Search
description: Sequential searching concepts and use cases.

questions.question: Linear search is also called:
questions.explanation: Linear search is also called Sequential Search because it examines elements in order, one after another.

questions.question: Which description best matches linear search?
options: It divides the data in half repeatedly
It finds the minimum element and moves it forward
It checks each element in order until it finds the target
It builds a sorted list one item at a time
questions.explanation: Linear search checks each element in sequence until the target is found or the list ends. It does not rely on sorting.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about linear search?
options: It can skip elements using a pivot
It makes no assumption about the order of the data
It eliminates half the data at each step
questions.explanation: Linear search works with both sorted and unsorted data because it looks at each item sequentially without assuming any order.

questions.question: When is linear search the best choice?
options: For small datasets or unsorted and frequently changing data
Only when data is stored in a tree
questions.explanation: Linear search is ideal for small or unsorted data and when the dataset changes often, avoiding the overhead of sorting.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
questions.explanation: In the worst case, linear search checks every element, giving it O(n) time complexity.

title: Binary Search
description: Divide and conquer searching on sorted data.

questions.question: What is the main requirement for binary search to work correctly?
options: The data must be in a linked list
The data must have no duplicates
The data must be in a tree
questions.explanation: Binary search requires sorted data because it decides whether to look left or right based on ordering.

questions.question: Which strategy best describes binary search?
questions.explanation: Binary search divides the search range in half repeatedly, making it a divide and conquer algorithm.

questions.question: If the target is smaller than the middle element in a sorted array, where does binary search continue?
questions.explanation: When the target is smaller than the middle, the algorithm searches the left half of the sorted array.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
questions.explanation: Binary search runs in O(log n), because each comparison halves the remaining search space.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of using binary search?
options: It requires more memory than linear search
It requires the dataset to be sorted before searching
questions.explanation: Binary search is fast, but it needs sorted data. Sorting can add extra work before the search begins.

title: Linear vs Binary Search
description: Compare the two core search methods.

questions.question: Which search algorithm works on UNSORTED data?
questions.explanation: Linear search works on unsorted data. Binary search requires sorted data to function correctly.

questions.question: Which algorithm is generally faster for very large sorted datasets?
options: It depends only on the language
questions.explanation: Binary search is faster for large sorted datasets because it reduces the search range exponentially.

questions.question: Which search method is easier to implement in code?
questions.explanation: Linear search is easier to implement because it only requires a simple loop over the collection.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'Use Linear Search for _____, use Binary Search for _____ ONLY when data is sorted.'
questions.explanation: The golden rule says use linear search for simplicity and binary search for efficiency when the data is already sorted.

title: Big-O Notation & Complexity
description: How algorithms scale as input grows.

questions.question: What does Big-O notation measure?
options: How the algorithm's work grows as input size increases
The amount of memory used by the CPU
The number of functions in a program
questions.explanation: Big-O measures how the work of an algorithm grows with input size, focusing on scalability rather than exact timing.

questions.question: Big-O notation provides what kind of bound?
questions.explanation: Big-O gives an upper bound on growth, describing the worst-case behavior of an algorithm.

questions.question: Rank these from fastest to slowest growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²).
questions.explanation: Constant time is fastest, followed by logarithmic, linear, and quadratic growth.

questions.question: Which complexity class means the algorithm takes the same amount of time no matter how much the input grows?
questions.explanation: O(1) means constant time — the runtime stays the same regardless of input size.

questions.question: What is the difference between Time Complexity and Space Complexity?
options: Time measures memory; space measures speed
Time measures speed; space measures memory usage
Time measures the number of variables; space measures number of functions
questions.explanation: Time Complexity describes how fast an algorithm runs; Space Complexity describes how much memory it requires.

questions.question: Why is Big-O important when selecting algorithms?
options: It gives the exact runtime for any input
It helps predict which algorithms will scale better as the dataset grows
It shows how pretty the code is
questions.explanation: Big-O helps choose algorithms that remain efficient as the input size increases, preventing slow behavior for large datasets.

questions.question: What is the fundamental rule of a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
options: Right child is always the root
questions.explanation: BST rule: left child values are less than or equal to the parent, and right child values are greater than or equal to the parent.

questions.question: In a BST, what does the performance of most operations depend on?
questions.explanation: Operations like search, insert, and delete depend on tree height. A shorter tree height means faster operations.

questions.question: Which traversal of a BST gives the nodes in sorted order?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal visits left child, root, then right child, producing sorted output for a BST.

questions.question: How do you find the minimum value in a BST?
questions.explanation: The minimum value in a BST resides in the leftmost node, because left children hold smaller values.

questions.question: What happens if elements are inserted in sorted order into a basic BST?
options: The tree becomes skewed and height grows to O(n)
questions.explanation: Inserting sorted data into a simple BST creates a skewed structure, similar to a linked list, which degrades performance to O(n).

title: Tree Traversal
description: Visit tree nodes in different orders.

questions.question: What is the order of Pre-order traversal?
questions.explanation: Pre-order traversal visits the current node first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.

questions.question: What is the order of Post-order traversal?
questions.explanation: Post-order traversal visits left subtree, then right subtree, then the current node last.

questions.question: Which traversal visits the root node first?
questions.explanation: Pre-order visits the root before its children, making root the first node visited.

questions.question: Which traversal visits the root node last?
questions.explanation: Post-order traversal processes the left and right subtrees before visiting the root last.

questions.question: Which traversal is most useful for evaluating expression trees where operators come after operands?
questions.explanation: Post-order traversal evaluates operands before the operator, which matches how expression trees should be evaluated.

title: Simple Sorting Algorithms
description: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort basics.

questions.question: What does Bubble Sort do during each pass?
options: Finds the minimum element and places it in front
Swaps adjacent elements that are in the wrong order
Inserts one element into the correct position
questions.explanation: Bubble Sort compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are out of order, gradually moving larger items toward the end.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort?
questions.explanation: Bubble Sort compares many pairs of adjacent elements, giving it O(n²) time complexity in the general case.

questions.question: How does Selection Sort arrange the data?
options: By finding the smallest element and placing it in the correct position
By inserting each element into an already sorted portion
By dividing the array into halves and merging
questions.explanation: Selection Sort repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next sorted position.

questions.question: Insertion Sort is best described as:
options: Finding the smallest element each time
Building a sorted portion by inserting each element into its correct position
questions.explanation: Insertion Sort builds a sorted section of the array by inserting each new element into the correct place among the sorted items.

questions.question: A real-life example of Insertion Sort is:
options: Picking the lowest score and placing it first
Sorting cards by inserting each new card into its position
questions.explanation: Inserting cards into the correct place among the cards already held mirrors the way Insertion Sort builds a sorted list one item at a time.

questions.question: Which simple sorting algorithms are in-place and do not need extra memory?
questions.explanation: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort all sort within the original array without requiring additional data structures.

title: Efficient Sorting Algorithms
description: Merge, Quick, and Heap Sort fundamentals.

questions.question: What strategy does Merge Sort use?
options: Divide and conquer with division and merging
questions.explanation: Merge Sort divides the array into halves, sorts each half, then merges the sorted parts — a divide and conquer method.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Merge Sort?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort runs in O(n log n) consistently because it divides the data and merges sorted halves.

questions.question: What is a key characteristic of Merge Sort compared to other O(n log n) algorithms?
options: It is stable and retains the relative order of equal elements
It always sorts in place without extra memory
questions.explanation: Merge Sort is stable, which means it preserves the original relative order of equal elements during sorting.

questions.question: How does Quick Sort work?
options: By finding the smallest item and moving it forward
By choosing a pivot, partitioning around it, and sorting recursively
By always selecting the largest remaining item
questions.explanation: Quick Sort chooses a pivot and partitions the array into values less than and greater than the pivot, then recursively sorts each partition.

questions.question: What is Quick Sort's average time complexity?
questions.explanation: Quick Sort usually runs in O(n log n) on average, which is why it is very fast in practice.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm uses a heap data structure?
questions.explanation: Heap Sort uses a heap, a priority-based tree structure, to repeatedly extract the highest or lowest element.

title: Sorting Algorithm Comparison
description: Compare speed, use cases, and trade-offs.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is easiest to understand but slowest for large data?
questions.explanation: Bubble Sort is conceptually simple but has O(n²) performance, making it very slow for large datasets.

questions.question: Which three sorting algorithms have O(n²) time complexity?
questions.explanation: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort are all simple O(n²) algorithms.

questions.question: Which three sorting algorithms have O(n log n) time complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, and Heap Sort all achieve O(n log n) performance in their efficient forms.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is known for needing extra memory to merge results?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort requires additional memory to merge sorted subarrays, even though it is stable and efficient.

questions.question: When would Quick Sort be preferred over Merge Sort?
options: When you need a stable sort
When memory is limited and in-place sorting is desired
When the data is already sorted
When the dataset is stored on disk
questions.explanation: Quick Sort is in-place and uses less extra memory than Merge Sort, making it a good choice when memory is scarce.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is best for data that is already mostly sorted?
questions.explanation: Insertion Sort performs very well on nearly sorted data and can approach O(n) time in the best case.

questions.question: What is an AVL Tree?
options: A tree where all nodes are red or black
A self-balancing BST with height difference limited to -1, 0, or +1
A multi-child tree used in databases
A tree with no balancing rule
questions.explanation: An AVL Tree is a self-balancing BST with a balance factor of -1, 0, or +1 at every node.

questions.question: What is the balance factor in an AVL Tree?
options: The number of nodes in the left subtree
The color assigned to each node
The height difference between left and right subtrees
The number of children per node
questions.explanation: The balance factor equals the height of the left subtree minus the height of the right subtree. AVL Trees keep it between -1 and +1.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of AVL Trees?
options: They keep tree height minimal for consistent speed
They use color rules instead of height rules
They store data only in leaves
questions.explanation: AVL Trees rebalance themselves to keep height small, which preserves fast and predictable search and update times.

questions.question: What is the best use case for AVL Trees?
options: Fast searches where reads are more common than writes
Storing data in leaf nodes only
questions.explanation: AVL Trees are ideal for fast searching when the tree is not modified constantly, because strict balancing costs extra rebalancing on writes.

questions.question: What makes a Red-Black Tree different from an AVL Tree?
options: Red-Black Trees use color rules instead of strict height balancing
Red-Black Trees can have more than two children
Red-Black Trees store data only in leaf nodes
questions.explanation: Red-Black Trees balance using color rules rather than enforcing a strict height difference, making them more flexible for frequent updates.

questions.question: Which rule is required in a Red-Black Tree?
options: No node can have two black children
No two red nodes can be adjacent
Each node must have exactly two children
questions.explanation: One key rule is that a red node cannot have a red parent or red child, so no two red nodes are adjacent.

questions.question: In a Red-Black Tree, every path from root to leaf must have the same number of:
questions.explanation: All root-to-leaf paths must contain the same number of black nodes, which helps maintain balance.

questions.question: Red-Black Trees are especially good when:
options: Reads are rare and writes are frequent
Searches must be the fastest possible no matter what
Data is stored on disk only
questions.explanation: Red-Black Trees handle frequent insertions and deletions efficiently by using flexible balancing rules that require fewer rotations than AVL Trees.

title: B-Trees and B+ Trees
description: Trees designed for databases and disk storage.

questions.question: What is a B-Tree?
options: A binary tree with exactly two children
A self-balancing tree with multiple keys and children designed to minimize disk reads
A tree where all data is stored in internal nodes
A tree that uses colors for balancing
questions.explanation: A B-Tree is a self-balancing tree with nodes that can contain multiple keys and children, optimized to reduce disk access.

questions.question: Where are B-Trees and B+ Trees commonly used?
questions.explanation: B-Trees and B+ Trees are widely used in databases and file systems because they handle large data efficiently with multi-level indexing.

questions.question: What makes B+ Trees different from B-Trees?
options: B+ Trees store data in internal nodes only
B+ Trees use color rules for balance
B+ Trees store all actual data in leaf nodes and link the leaves
questions.explanation: B+ Trees keep actual records in linked leaf nodes while internal nodes contain only keys for indexing.

questions.question: In a B+ Tree, internal nodes typically store:
questions.explanation: Internal nodes in a B+ Tree store keys used for navigation while the actual data remains in the leaf nodes.

questions.question: Why are B-Trees designed to minimize disk reads?
options: Disk reads are faster than memory reads
Each node stores many keys, reducing tree height and disk accesses
They store only one key per node
They do not use any indexing
questions.explanation: Because each node can hold many keys, B-Trees have fewer levels, which reduces the number of expensive disk accesses during search.

title: Tree Structures Comparison
description: Compare AVL, Red-Black, and B-tree families.

questions.question: Which tree is strictly balanced for maximum search speed?
questions.explanation: AVL Trees enforce strict height balance, giving them very fast search performance at the cost of more rebalancing.

questions.question: Which tree is best for frequent insertions and deletions?
questions.explanation: Red-Black Trees use more flexible balancing rules, making them efficient for operations that modify the tree often.

questions.question: Which tree structure is used for large-scale indexing and database systems?
questions.explanation: B+ Trees are commonly used in databases and file systems because they support large indexes and efficient sequential access.

questions.question: Which structure is described by 'multi-children nodes'?
questions.explanation: B-Trees can have many children per node, unlike binary trees which can only have up to two children.

questions.question: The quote 'Same data, different structure = different performance' means:
options: All data structures perform the same
The right structure improves access and operations
questions.explanation: Different structures organize the same information in different ways, which affects speed and efficiency.

questions.question: In a tree, what is the ROOT?
options: The topmost node with no parent
A node with exactly two children
questions.explanation: The root is the topmost node of a tree and has no parent.

questions.question: What is a LEAF node?
options: A node with exactly two children
questions.explanation: A leaf node has no children and appears at the end of a branch.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Binary Tree and a BST?
options: Binary trees allow any order; BSTs enforce left ≤ parent ≤ right
Binary trees are always sorted; BSTs are not
BSTs can have more than two children
questions.explanation: A binary tree only limits children to two per node, while a BST also enforces an ordering rule among node values.

questions.question: What does the height of a tree represent?
options: The number of nodes in the root
The length of the longest path from root to a leaf
The number of children each node has
questions.explanation: Tree height is the length of the longest path from the root down to any leaf, and it affects search performance.

title: Big Picture: Data Structures + Algorithms
description: How structure and efficiency work together.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Data Structures, Algorithms, and Complexity?
options: Data structures organize data, algorithms process it, and complexity measures efficiency
Algorithms are more important than structure
questions.explanation: Data structures organize data, algorithms operate on it, and complexity measures how efficiently those algorithms run.

questions.question: What does 'Same data, different structure = different performance' mean?
options: How data is stored affects how fast it can be used
Different structures always give the same speed
questions.explanation: The way data is structured changes access and operation costs, so choosing the right data structure matters.

questions.question: Why is sorting a foundation in computer science?
options: It is only used for display purposes
Sorted data enables faster searching and many algorithms rely on it
Sorting is optional in real systems
questions.explanation: Sorted data makes searching faster and is often assumed by many algorithms and system designs.

questions.question: What do balanced trees like AVL and Red-Black Trees provide?
options: Consistent performance by keeping height low
questions.explanation: Balanced trees keep their height small, helping operations stay fast and consistent rather than degrading on unbalanced data.

questions.question: Why is Big-O important for scalability?
options: It shows how algorithms behave as data grows larger
It tells the exact runtime for every input size
It only applies to small data
It measures the size of the code
questions.explanation: Big-O describes how performance grows with input size, making it essential for choosing algorithms that scale well.
